newsitem.title: INDIA: Unseasonal rains could damage Indian wheat crop.
newsitem.headline: Unseasonal rains could damage Indian wheat crop.

text.p: India, forced to import wheat to augment domestic supplies, could face problems if unseasonal rains in the north continued, threatening the wheat crop, analysts and officials said on Friday.
The main wheat-growing states of Punjab, Haryana and Uttar Pradesh have been lashed by heavy rains accompanied by strong winds during the week, delaying harvesting in some areas.

"The rains would affect the wheat crop in many ways. The standing crop will be affected, the threshing will get delayed and the harvested seed will get a mold," said S. M. Virmani, an agriculture expert with the International Crops Research Institute for the Semi-Arid Tropics (ICRISAT).
Punjab and Haryana together produce about 60 percent of the country's total wheat output.
The Agriculture Ministry has forecast the 1996/97 (July-June) wheat crop at 64.5 million tonnes against 62.6 million in 1995/96.
Analysts said the wheat harvest was in full swing in the central state of Madhya Pradesh and western state of Gujarat, and was picking up in the northern states.
They said if the rains continue over the weekend it could damage the wheat crop.
Virmani said the rains would affect the quality of wheat and hit small farmers who do not have sophisticated machines to do the entire operation of cutting, thrashing and drying in one go.
Officials of the Indian Council of Agriculture Research (ICAR) said they were awaiting information on the extent of rains and their impact on the wheat growing regions.
"Rain at this stage is undesirable for the wheat crop," said one ICAR official.
But M.S. Bhatia, advisor in the Agriculture Ministry, said the weather was improving and heavy damage is caused only when the rains persist.
India banned exports of wheat in September 1996 when stock limits fell to very low levels due to four million tonnes less procurement by state agencies than estimated.

Food Minister Devendra Prasad Yadav told parliament in March that India's wheat stocks on April 1 were projected at 2.72 million tonnes, down one million tonnes from the buffer stock norms of 3.7 million tonnes set by the government.
In December India authorised the state-run State Trading Corporation (STC) to import two million tonnes of wheat to build stocks and check rising prices.

A U.S. agricultural attache report released in Washington on Thursday said the Indian government recently bought 1.0 million tonnes of Australian wheat, bringing its combined purchases since December 1996 to nearly 2.7 million tonnes.
It said STC might be interested in an additional 500,000 to 800,000 tonnes if prices were attractive.
STC's initial import allocation was for 2.0 million tonnes but this has reportedly been revised to 3.5 million tonnes, the report said.
STC officials in New Delhi could not be reached to confirm the report.
Meteorological Department officials said north western India had been getting heavy rains since April 1 and scattered rains had occurred in almost half of the country.
But they said rains in the northern belt were expected to decrease from Saturday onwards.
"It will be affecting the wheat crops. Strong winds and rains mean plants may not be erect. Pest and disease chances are there," said A.V.R. Krishna Rao of the Indian Meteorlogical Department.
Rao said cloudy weather over the last week was not conducive since warm temperatures were needed during harvest time.
